grammar: The object is fronted: 'and from the tree ... not you shall eat from it'. The same tree is named with a repeated pronoun, וּמֵעֵץ ... מִמֶּנּוּ.
לֹא תֹאכַל is an imperfect with 'not', a prohibition (compare 'you must not'), in contrast to the permission of 2:16.
בְּיוֹם אֲכׇלְךָ is a temporal clause built on a construct noun and an infinitive construct with a suffix.
מוֹת תָּמוּת joins the infinitive absolute to the finite verb for certainty ('you will surely die'). The etnaḥta falls on מִמֶּנּוּ and divides prohibition from reason; silluq closes the verse.
segments.note: The English keeps the order 'from the tree ... you must not eat from it', as the Hebrew fronts the object. 'Evil' is chosen for רָע (it is the noun here, paired with good). The sense of מוֹת תָּמוּת is left as 'surely die', without saying when death comes; Ramban and Radak read the day as the time at which one becomes liable to death.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: after saying 'from the tree' the word מִמֶּנּוּ is added to make it clear, like 'she opened it and saw him, the child' (Ex 2:6); or it means 'not even a little of it'. The man was full of knowledge, since he named the animals; only the knowledge of good and evil in one matter he lacked. The English keeps the double 'from the tree ... from it'.
Ramban: the prohibition is of the fruit, since the tree itself is not eaten; compare 3:3 'from the fruit of the tree'.
Ramban: 'on the day you eat' means the time when one becomes liable to death, as in 1 Kings 2:42; it does not mean he dies within the day.

apparatus: The pack parses the suffix of מִמֶּנּוּ as 1st person plural; the form is the usual 3rd masc. sing. 'from it' with a doubled nun, and the English follows the sense.

segments.literal: and-said the-LORD God not good to-be the-human by-himself I-will-make for-him help like-opposite-him

imperfect, 1st sing., cohortative sense of resolve
'like his opposite': כְּ + נֶגֶד + suffix, 'what faces him, matches him'

phrases.english: for the human to be alone

grammar: לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ: an infinitive construct with its own subject, הָאָדָם, after a predicate adjective.
אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ is a 1st person imperfect, here a resolve of the speaker ('I will make').
עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is two words: 'a help' and 'like his counterpart'; כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is not a verb but a prepositional phrase.
The etnaḥta falls on לְבַדּוֹ and divides the statement from the resolve.
segments.note: 'Corresponding to him' keeps the meaning 'a match, what stands opposite him' (Ibn Ezra, Sforno: equal to him). Rashi's reading 'opposite him, to fight' is kept in the commentary entry.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'not good' so that people would not say there are two powers, the Holy One alone above with no partner, and this one alone below with no partner. The English keeps the plain 'not good for the human to be alone'.
Rashi: if he is worthy, a help; if not, 'against him', to fight. The English keeps the neutral 'corresponding to him' and records the second reading.
Ibn Ezra: the meaning of 'not good' is said of the human; it is not good for him.
Ibn Ezra: 'help' has the sense of 'two are better than one' (Eccl 4:9); a helper in company.
Radak repeats the reading 'if worthy, a help; if not, against him' (Gen. Rabbah 17).

apparatus: WLC reads אֶעֱשֶׂהּ for MAM אֶעֱשֶׂה (2:18.9, vowels); the sense is unchanged.

grammar: וַיִּצֶר is a wayyiqtol of יצר (the yod of the root is dropped in writing, as Radak notes); the sequence continues the narrative but does not fix a new moment (compare 'had formed').
לִרְאוֹת מַה־יִּקְרָא־לוֹ: purpose, with an indirect question, 'to see what he would call it'.

וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא־לוֹ הָאָדָם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְׁמוֹ is a hard construction: 'and all which the human would call to it, a living being, that is its name'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both read נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה as the thing named.
Wordplay: אֲדָמָה (ground), אָדָם (human).
segments.note: For the last clause the English follows the agreed reading of Rashi and Ibn Ezra: 'each living creature the human called, that was its name'. Ramban gives a different reading (the human calls each kind 'a living being' like himself, and so finds none a help); it is kept in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'formed' is the same act as the 'making' of the beasts above; Scripture adds that birds were made from the ground (the swamp), and that they were brought to the human the same day to be named. In aggadah, 'form' means 'subdue'.
Rashi: rearrange it and explain: every living being that the human would call by a name, that is its name for ever.
Ibn Ezra: the lamed of לוֹ draws itself and another with it: 'whatever the human called it as a living being'; it adds clarity, like 'she opened it and saw him' (Ex 2:6).
Ramban offers a reading connecting the clause with the search for a helper: whichever kind the human calls 'living being' like himself would be the helper; he found none.

segments.english: The human gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for the human he did not find a helper corresponding to him.
segments.literal: and-called the-human names to-every-of the-livestock and-to-bird-of the-heavens and-to-every-of animal-of the-field and-for-human not he-found help like-opposite-him

construct, collective

grammar: The 'to' of לְכָל־הַבְּהֵמָה governs the next noun too: Ibn Ezra reads 'to all the livestock and to the birds', with the lamed 'drawing' the next noun along.
Anarthrous וּלְאָדָם: Ibn Ezra reads 'and for himself', as the Hebrew idiom puts the name of a person for the person. Rashi has the human speak of himself.
The subject of לֹא־מָצָא is the human, not the LORD God (Ibn Ezra calls the reading with the LORD as subject 'far').
The zaqef gadol on וּלְאָדָם marks the turn from the naming to the lack.
segments.note: 'For the human' follows the decision on הָאָדָם and records that אָדָם is without the article here; Ibn Ezra's 'for himself' and a proper-name reading are kept in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Rashi: when each kind was brought, male and female, he said: all have a mate and I have none; at once, 'And the LORD God cast a deep sleep'.
Ibn Ezra: לכל הבהמה also draws itself and another with it; it means 'and to the birds of the sky', as in Deut 33:6 and Prov 30:3.

Ibn Ezra: 'and for the human he found none' means 'for himself he found none', as Hebrew idiom has it (1 Sam 12:11); he rejects the reading in which the LORD is the subject. Here he adds that the birds were formed from the ground, and above from the waters, since from both.
Ramban discusses the placing of the naming in the account of the helper.

apparatus: Anarthrous אָדָם (2:20.11): Ibn Ezra 'for himself'; as a name 'for Adam' is possible (decision: 'the human' where doubtful; not 'Adam' before 4:25).

and he took one of his sides
and closed up flesh in its place

grammar: הִפִּיל תַּרְדֵּמָה is a Hifil of נפל with an object: 'made a deep sleep fall' on the human; Ibn Ezra notes the 'heavy' stem.
וַיִּישַׁן, וַיִּקַּח, וַיִּסְגֹּר: a run of wayyiqtols narrates the operation.
אַחַת מִצַּלְעֹתָיו: the numeral is feminine to agree with צֵלָע; the partitive מִ gives 'one of his sides'.
תַּחְתֶּנָּה has a nun added to the feminine suffix (Radak, Ibn Ezra), as תַּחְתֶּיהָ.
segments.note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that צֵלָע is 'side' here (Rashi: 'his sides', as in 'the side of the tabernacle'; Ibn Ezra: 'side'). The English follows: 'one of his sides'. 'Rib' (Targum Onkelos עלעא, Radak's second view) is kept in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Rashi: מִצַּלְעֹתָיו means 'from his sides', as 'the side of the tabernacle' (Ex 26); this is the saying 'two faces were created'.
Rashi: וַיִּסְגֹּר is 'the place of the cut'.
Rashi: he slept and then took, so that he would not see the piece of flesh from which she was made and be repelled; it bears on motive, not on the words.
Ibn Ezra: וַיַּפֵּל is from the heavy (Hifil) stem.
Ibn Ezra: תַּרְדֵּמָה is more than sleep, and sleep more than slumber; the ת is added.
Ibn Ezra: there were two 'sides', as 'the second side of the tabernacle' (Ex 26:20); the word is feminine; the sense is 'side'.
Ibn Ezra: תַּחְתֶּנָּה is 'its place', a singular with a nun added.
Radak: some say two faces joined back to back, with 'rib' as 'side'; some say literally 'rib' (as Onkelos עַלְעָא).

apparatus: 'Rib' (Onkelos, Radak's second view) is the common rendering of צֵלָע; the English follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra's 'side'.

segments.english: The LORD God built the side that he had taken from the human into a woman, and brought her to the human.
segments.literal: and-built the-LORD God OBJ-the-side which he-took from-the-human to-woman and-brought-her to-the-human

grammar: וַיִּבֶן is a wayyiqtol of בנה in the Qal ('built'); Ibn Ezra notes both a Hifil and a Qal sense for such forms; the verb takes the side as object.
לְאִשָּׁה: the preposition ל marks the result of the building, 'into a woman' (Rashi), not a purpose clause.
אֲשֶׁר־לָקַח is a perfect in a relative clause, a pluperfect in sense ('had taken').
The telisha qetana (twice) on וַיִּבֶן, then qadma and darga, link the subject and divide off the long object.
segments.note: Rashi's 'built' as 'in the form of a building, wide below and narrow above' bears on the picture of the verb and is kept in the commentary entry; the English uses 'built' as the plain word.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'built' as a building, wide below and narrow above, to receive the child, as a granary for wheat is wide below and narrow above.
Rashi: לְאִשָּׁה means 'to be a woman', as 'Gideon made it into an ephod'.
Ibn Ezra: וַיִּבֶן is of the Hifil, and also of the Qal, as וַיִּפֶן, וַיִּקֶן.

Ibn Ezra: either he thought, on waking and seeing her, that she was brought as the animals were, and Scripture speaks of his thought; or she was built outside the garden and then brought; when he looked he knew she had been cut from him.

phrases.english: This one shall be called woman

grammar: זֹאת הַפַּעַם: 'this one, the time', hence 'this time'; the revia and zaqef divide the line into two cola.
עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי: two parallel lines, with a verbless clause: the first colon names bone, the second flesh.
אִשָּׁה and אִישׁ: a wordplay. Rashi: the Holy Tongue is the language of creation; Ibn Ezra explains the dagesh in שׁ as in place of the yod of אִישׁ.
יִקָּרֵא is a Nifal imperfect; לֻקְּחָה is a Pual perfect (WLC vowels לֻקֳחָה, MAM לֻקְחָה).
segments.note: 'This time' is the plain sense; Rashi's homily (the human had come on every beast and was not satisfied) is not adopted. Radak: this time (not the first, when the animals were brought).

commentary.summary: Rashi (Yevamot 63a): this teaches that the human came upon every beast and animal and was not satisfied; a homily, not the plain sense.
Rashi: a play on words (אִישׁ, אִשָּׁה): from here the world was created in the Holy Tongue.
Ibn Ezra: then he said: this time I have found a help corresponding to me, like me, since from me she was; and the Lilith story is homily.
Ibn Ezra: וְלָזֹאת means 'because of this one', as 'say of me, He is my brother' (Gen 20:13).
Ibn Ezra: the dagesh in the שׁ of אִשָּׁה replaces the silent yod of אִישׁ, and perhaps it is dagesh so as not to be mixed with אִישָׁהּ, 'her husband'; compare נשים from אנוש.
Ibn Ezra: יִקָּרֵא means 'on a name', that is 'be called by name'.

apparatus: WLC reads לֻקֳחָה for MAM לֻקְחָה (vowels, 2:23.14); the same word.

segments.english: Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
segments.literal: upon-so he-leaves man OBJ his-father and-OBJ his-mother and-clings to-his-wife and-they-become to-flesh one

grammar: עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ: an imperfect after 'therefore' states a general rule, hence the present tense of the English.
וְדָבַק and וְהָיוּ are weqatal forms that continue the imperfect; the subject changes from 'a man' to 'they' (the man and his wife).
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד: 'into one flesh', ל marking the result; compare Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the sense of unity.
The pashta on כֵּן and the zaqef on אִישׁ divide the verse; the etnaḥta falls on אִמּוֹ.
segments.note: The tense is present because the verse states a rule that follows from what was just done. Rashi's homily about the prohibition of incest is a legal derivation and does not bear on the English. 'One flesh' is read, as Ibn Ezra reads it, as 'as if they were one'; Rashi's 'the child' and the sense of procreation are kept in the commentary entry.

commentary.summary: Rashi (Sanhedrin 57b): the holy spirit says this to forbid incest to the sons of Noah; a derived law, not the plain sense.
Rashi (Sanhedrin 58a): the child is formed from both of them, and there their flesh becomes one; this is an alternative sense of 'one flesh', not adopted here.
Ibn Ezra: 'they become one flesh' as if they were one, or that they would be like one as they were; those who say they beget one are far from the plain sense. The English follows the first reading.
Ramban rejects Rashi's reading (animals too become one flesh in their young) and takes 'one flesh' to mean the clinging of man to wife as to his own flesh.
